vignette:
He is a 35-year-old South Asian man who comes across as careful and composed at first, the kind of person who speaks in measured sentences and keeps his hands folded when he is trying to stay organized. He is married and works as a tax consultant now, but his life changed during the months he spent as a relief worker in a war zone, where routine disappeared and every day felt governed by noise, fear, and the need to keep moving. He describes arriving with a clear sense of purpose. He wanted to help, to be useful, to do something practical in the face of suffering. At the time, that intention gives him energy. He remembers carrying supplies, checking lists, translating for families, and trying to stay focused on tasks because focusing on tasks was safer than looking too closely at what was happening around him.

The first event that stays lodged in him is the day a convoy is hit nearby. He is not directly injured, but he sees enough to understand how quickly ordinary life can break apart. He recalls dust, screaming, and the disorienting sense that the ground itself has become unstable. After that, he begins sleeping lightly, always half-listening for the next impact. He tells himself that vigilance is part of the job, yet even then he notices how his body never fully settles. His shoulders stay tense. His stomach tightens when vehicles backfire. He becomes aware that he is counting exits, memorizing the safest places to crouch, and planning routes through rooms before he even enters them.

As the months go on, the work becomes more morally and emotionally draining. He is often with families after bombings or displacement, trying to hand out food, water, and medication while listening to people ask questions he cannot answer. He sees children who no longer cry because they seem too exhausted to cry, and he describes that as the part that haunts him most. There are times when he has to keep moving while others grieve. He learns to shut down during the day so he can function, but the shutting down does not end when the shift ends. At night, when he finally lies down, scenes return with a force that feels involuntary. He sees injured bodies, hears fragments of voices, and wakes with a jolt, disoriented, as if he has been dropped back into danger.

When he returns home, he expects relief, but instead he finds that the world feels strangely artificial. His wife is glad to have him back, and he loves her presence, yet he is often detached, as if part of him is still elsewhere. He avoids talking about what he saw because once he starts, he worries he will not stop. He does not watch news coverage about conflict because images can arrive too quickly and too vividly. He notices that he sits with his back to walls in restaurants and that he scans crowded streets before crossing them. Loud sounds pull him into an immediate alertness he cannot control. He becomes irritable in ways that surprise him. Small frustrations at home or at work can trigger a surge of anger, followed by shame. He does not like who he becomes in those moments, and that dislike deepens his isolation.

At his job as a tax consultant, he is respected for being precise and reliable, but he experiences his office as a place where he must constantly prove to himself that he can still think clearly. He works hard to keep his attention on calculations, deadlines, and regulations because numbers are orderly in a way life in the war zone was not. Even so, concentration does not come easily. He rereads the same lines, loses track of details, and sometimes stares at a spreadsheet without absorbing it. He worries about making mistakes, then worries about worrying. He has become the kind of man who checks things repeatedly, not because he is naturally exacting, but because uncertainty now feels dangerous.

He also notices that his emotions have narrowed. He can still care deeply for his wife and family, but he feels less able to access pleasure. He exercises because he knows it helps him sleep, yet even on calm days he carries a muted sense of threat, as though the worst part of the war never fully ended and simply followed him home in quieter form. Still, there are brief moments when he can feel something like relief: when he is walking in the early morning, when his wife speaks gently without asking for an explanation, when he finishes a difficult client file and realizes he has stayed present long enough to complete it. These moments do not erase what happened, but they show how much effort it takes for him to remain in the ordinary world, one careful hour at a time.
